newsitem.title: USA: Blue-chip stocks extend losing streak to third day.
newsitem.headline: Blue-chip stocks extend losing streak to third day.

text.p: Blue-chip stocks closed lower for a third straight session Wednesday as investors wondered whether the market was heading for a big pre-election correction after sweeping to a series of record highs last week.
The Dow Jones industrial average ended 25.34 points lower at 6,036.46 after being down nearly 70 points at one time.
In the broader market, declining issues led advances 1,261 to 1,061 on active volume of 439 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.

Meanwhile, a recovery in the recently battered high technology stocks helped shore up the Nasdaq Composite index, which ended up 7.88 points to 1,227.88 after losing a total of 22 points on Monday and Tuesday.
"The techs are looking strong as we close out the day. Intel, Microsoft, Cisco and IBM have had very nice rebounds," said Peter Canelo, chief investment strategist at Dean Witter.
"The correction for techs in terms of time may go on for awhile but it's mostly over in terms of price," he said.
Analysts said the market was looking to the November elections.
"What we are seeing is a discounting process ahead of the election in November," said Joseph Barthel, chief investment strategist at Fahnestock & Co.
He said traders were considering the possibility of Democrats riding President Clinton's coattails to retake one or both houses of Congress.
"Wall Street likes Clinton with a Republican Congress," Barthel said.
Among technology stocks, International Business Machines ended up 2-1/8 to 129-1/8, Intel added 3-7/8 to 109-3/8, Cisco was up 1-5/8 to 62-7/8 and Microsoft rose 2-1/8 to 129-1/8.
Electronic Data Systems Corp. plunged 11-1/2, or 19 percent, to 48 after the company said slack orders and lower federal government spending would pressure its growth in the fourth quarter.

"EDS was the story of the day," said Thom Brown, a managing director of Rutherford Brown & Catherwood. "There was a gross overreaction to their news. The market is most punishing when it comes to any doubts about the outlook."
Computer Sciences, EDS's chief rival, lost 2-1/4 to 77-5/8.

Conrail soared 11-1/8 to 95-5/8 after Norfolk Southern launched a $100 per share cash offer for the company in a bid intended to derail CSX Corp.'s friendly $92.50 a share merger pact. CSX slipped 3/4 to 45-1/2 and Norfolk Southern lost 3/8 to 94-1/8.

AT&T lost 2 to 37-7/8 after the telecommunications giant ended weeks of speculation and named R.R. Donnelley & Sons' Chairman John Walter as its new president and chief operating officer. Walter will eventually succeed Robert Allen as chairman and chief executive.
SBC Warburg downgraded AT&T's stock based on Walter's appointment, saying it had expected a "fresh face with a well-known high tech resume."
Netscape rallied 5-3/8 to 49-7/8 on Tuesday's strong quarterly profit report.

Boston Beer sank 3-3/8 to 12-5/8 on news that orders for its microbrew were lower than expected. Other microbrewery stocks also tumbled with Redhook Ale off 1-5/16 to 14-11/16, Pete's Brewing off 3/8 to 7-3/8, Pyramid Breweries off 1/4 to 5-1/2 and Nor'Wester Brewing down 5/8 to 4-1/8.
United Auto Group surged 4-7/8 to 34-7/8 in its Wall Street debut. The company operates franchised automotive and light truck dealerships and related businesses.
The Standard & Poor's composite index of 500 stocks rose 0.70 of a point to 707.27. The American Stock Exchange index lost 2.56 to 570.73.
The NYSE Composite index of all listed common stocks fell 0.31 to 375.91. The average share was down 3 cents.
The Wilshire Associates Equity Index -- the market value of NYSE, American and Nasdaq issues -- was 6,880.595 up 0.335 or 0.01 percent.
